title_en: The Tradition You Imagine Is Younger Than Coca-Cola
excerpt_en: Coca-Cola was born in 1886. The bubbling red-oil mala hotpot you think Sichuan has eaten for centuries took shape in the 1980s — nearly a hundred years younger than Coke.
body_en:
Coca-Cola was born in 1886. The bubbling red-oil, numbing-spicy hotpot that you imagine Sichuan and Chongqing have eaten for centuries took shape in the 1980s — nearly one hundred years younger than Coke.

Start with a question: before the 1980s, when cooking oil was desperately scarce, how did Sichuan people eat heavy-oil mala hotpot? The answer: they didn't. Before the 1980s, Sichuan simply had no such thing as a hotpot of rolling red oil famous for its numbing spice. To be clear, 'hotpot' here does not mean 'cooking things in a pot' — humans have done that since civilization began. It means the beef-tallow red broth served everywhere today.

First, do the math: where would the oil come from?

A red-oil hotpot base is, at its core, oil. But in the 1960s and 70s, urban residents' cooking oil was rationed: most people received five liang (250 grams) per person per month, and in provinces like Liaoning and Anhui, only three or four liang. A Shenyang chronicle of 1966–1985 records the city announcing that from October of one year, the oil ration would drop from five liang to three. With three liang of oil a month, you counted the drops going into a wok. What was left to build a pot of beef-tallow broth?

So before reform and opening, Sichuan and Chongqing had only plain-water 'vegetarian' hotpots. Even into the 1980s, oil stayed scarce, and hotpot ran on recycled broth — old oil used again and again, ingredients reused — perfectly normal for the era, and many regions had similar wisdom. Shaanxi's Guanzhong region had its 'soup-poured noodles': served only at weddings and funerals, a bowl held a few strands of noodle in mostly sour, fragrant hot soup. When a guest finished, the leftover broth was collected, poured back into the big pot, and ladled out again for the next bowl — locals called it 'saliva noodles.' In modern language: the sharing economy.

Before 1980, Chengdu had no hotpot

An old Chengdu architect wrote in his memoir: Chengdu had no hotpot. He arrived in Chengdu in 1977 and left for Hong Kong in 1987; in ten whole years he never once ate hotpot. What Chengdu had then were tripe shops, whose format resembled Beijing's instant-boiled mutton.

Those tripe shops are the traceable source of Sichuan-style hotpot. They began as food for boatmen and salt workers. A boat cannot host a proper stove, so a small brazier and one pot, everything boiled together, was the easiest way. Ancient salt works used oxen to haul brine; every month some oxen died of exhaustion. The beef went to the rich; the offal was eaten by the salt workers or sold to boatmen. Salt works were collective labor — dozens of men finishing heavy work and eating together — and one big boiled pot was again the easiest answer.

Honestly, calling this boiled food 'hotpot' is a stretch; it is closer to the Northeast's big mixed stews or Beijing's braised offal pots. It is just that Sichuan-Chongqing hotpot is so famous now that it needs an origin story — and the origin must not come from somewhere else. In 1920, Chongqing's Bai Letian opened for business: the earliest verifiable tripe hotpot shop. Note the year — 1920. Coca-Cola had already been selling for 34 years. As late as 1982, a Chinese food magazine introducing Sichuan tripe hotpot recorded the shops' final form: they were still using the copper pot of Beijing's boiled-mutton style.

The real hotpot template was in Beijing

Donglaishun, the Beijing boiled-mutton house founded in 1903, is the form closest to how people eat hotpot today. Most other places calling themselves 'hotpot' were really stews — people simply did not draw the distinction back then; even Korea's sinseollo and Japan's sukiyaki were once given the hotpot name in China.

The Qing-dynasty gourmet Yuan Mei was an opponent of hotpot, using it as a negative example in his food writings: using a hotpot for winter banquets, steaming and bubbling in front of guests, is truly detestable; every dish has its own proper heat — some gentle, some fierce, some to be added, some removed — and forcing them all through one pot of fire leaves nothing to say about flavor.

There was also a more practical barrier: fuel. The rich had endless charcoal; ordinary people could not afford to keep a pot simmering for a long, leisurely meal. In an age of expensive fuel, hotpot was never common folks' food. So saying that Sichuan's boiled tripe imitated Beijing's boiled mutton is no exaggeration at all.

The red-oil base is an invention of the 1980s

Life kept getting better. By 1983, Sichuan-Chongqing tripe hotpot had begun using pre-fried base — but even then, most of the right to add beef tallow still sat with the diner: you seasoned the broth to taste, adding salt and tallow yourself, with a dipping dish of sesame oil and MSG on the side. The fully shop-prepared, red-oil-rolling broth of today was only a matter of time.

Common sense tells the story: without a great abundance of material goods, nobody in their right mind would burn that much beef tallow on a pot base. And old merchants understood the sharing economy early: ordinary families rarely deep-fried dough sticks at home, because a big pot of oil was beyond any one household — but a street stall could spread the cost of that expensive oil across hundreds of customers. Old oil, old braising liquid, old hotpot broth: all of it was the wisdom of pooling resources to taste a little oil in an age of scarcity.

Closing

So the story that 'Sichuan and Chongqing have loved red-oil hotpot since ancient times' splits into two halves. One half is what poverty produced — offal, big pots, recycled oil. The other half is what prosperity invented — a red-oil base with tallow to spare, forty years old at most. Next time someone tells you about a tradition 'since ancient times,' think of Coca-Cola first: plenty of revered traditions are younger than it is.

(Compiled from a video by Douyin creator 'Tomato on the Road'; the historical details and dates are that author's research.)
